title: Chapter 12 — Why The Americans Raise Some Monuments So Insignificant, And Others So Important
paragraphs: I have just noted that in democratic ages monuments of the arts tend to become more numerous and less important. Now I must point out the exception to this rule. In a democratic community individuals are very powerless, but the State that represents them all, and contains them all in its grasp, is very powerful. Nowhere do citizens appear as insignificant as in a democratic nation; nowhere does the nation itself appear greater, or can the mind more easily take in a wide general view of it. In democratic communities the imagination contracts when men consider themselves; it expands indefinitely when they think of the State. That is why the same men who live on a small scale in narrow dwellings often aspire to gigantic splendor in erecting their public monuments.

The Americans traced out the circuit of an immense city on the site they intended to make their capital, but which up to now is hardly more densely populated than Pontoise—though, according to them, it will one day contain a million inhabitants. They have already uprooted trees for ten miles around, so that the trees would not interfere with the future citizens of this imaginary metropolis. They have erected a magnificent palace for Congress in the center of the city and given it the pompous name of the Capitol. The several States of the Union are every day planning and building prodigious undertakings for themselves, which would astonish the engineers of the great European nations. Thus democracy not only leads men to a vast number of inconsequential productions; it also leads them to raise some monuments on the largest scale. But between these two extremes there is a blank. A few scattered remains of enormous buildings can therefore teach us nothing about the social condition and the institutions of the people who raised them. I may add—though the remark carries me outside my subject—that they do not give us a better knowledge of a people's greatness, its civilization, or its real prosperity either. Whenever a power of any kind can make a whole people cooperate in a single undertaking, that power, with a little knowledge and a great deal of time, will succeed in obtaining something enormous from the cooperation of efforts so multiplied. But this does not lead to the conclusion that the people was very happy, very enlightened, or even very strong.

The Spaniards found the city of Mexico full of magnificent temples and vast palaces, but that did not prevent Cortés from conquering the Mexican Empire with 600 foot soldiers and sixteen horses. If the Romans had been better acquainted with the laws of hydraulics, they would not have constructed all the aqueducts that surround the ruins of their cities—they would have made better use of their power and wealth. If they had invented the steam engine, perhaps they would not have extended to the farthest corners of their empire those long artificial roads called Roman roads. These things are at once the splendid memorials of their ignorance and of their greatness. A people that leaves no other trace of its path than a few lead pipes in the ground and a few iron rails on its surface might have been more the master of nature than the Romans.
